questions.passage:
Text 1
Critic Anselm Pryor faults Nadia Okonjo's novel The Lantern Year for its narrator, a retired schoolteacher whose account of a village scandal contradicts itself repeatedly. Dates shift, a conversation is described twice in incompatible ways, and the narrator insists on her own innocence while revealing details only the guilty party could know. Such inconsistencies, Pryor argues, leave readers with nothing solid to hold on to and suggest an author who lost control of her material.

Text 2
In The Lantern Year, Okonjo gives readers a narrator they cannot trust, and the novel is richer for it. The contradictions in the schoolteacher's story are too carefully placed to be accidents: each one appears just where her account most needs to protect her. Readers who notice them are drawn into the work of reconstructing what really happened, piecing together the truth from the very gaps the narrator tries to cover.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Pryor's criticism in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that the narrator's account is inconsistent but arguing that such inconsistencies are rare in Okonjo's other works
By arguing that the narrator's account is in fact consistent and that Pryor has misread the novel's timeline
By contending that the feature Pryor views as a flaw is a deliberate technique that engages readers in actively interpreting the story
By claiming that the novel's appeal depends mainly on its portrayal of village life rather than on its narrator

questions.passage:
Text 1

With a shell that measured 1.7 meters, the extinct mollusk Parapuzosia seppenradensis is the largest ammonite in the fossil record. Ever since fossilized remains of this large ammonite were first discovered in 1895, scientists have been perplexed by its size. After examining 154 ammonite fossils including P. seppenradensis fossils from England and Parapuzosia leptophylla (a smaller ammonite species) fossils from Mexico, paleontologist Christina Ifrim, Nils Schorndorf, and colleagues concluded that P. seppenradensis may have evolved from P. leptophylla and gradually increased in size as larger ammonites were better able to escape being preyed on by mosasaurs.

Text 2

Christina Ifrim and her team have expanded our understanding of the evolutionary history of ammonites in general, but their study has some gaps that will require additional research to fill. For instance, there’s evidence that mosasaurs preyed on ammonites, but there’s no direct evidence that they interacted specifically with P. seppenradensis.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely characterize the study conducted by Ifrim, Schorndorf, and colleagues in Text 1?
options: It is useful for the field as a whole, but a portion of it might be unfounded.
It is likely to become outdated quickly, but it features an impressive amount of data.
It is correct with regard to P. seppenradensis, but its claims about P. leptophylla are likely overstated.
It is relevant to the study of ammonites, but it overlooks the evolutionary history of mosasaurs.

Text 1
Companies have launched thousands of small satellites into low orbit to provide internet service, and many more are planned. Astronomer Chiara Bellini, who works at an observatory in Chile, reports that these satellites reflect sunlight and leave bright streaks across telescope images. She argues that they pose a serious threat to astronomy from the ground and that the number of launches should be limited.

Text 2
Engineer Tomasz Wójcik notes that satellite makers have begun using darker coatings and sunshades, which make newer satellites noticeably fainter. In addition, software can now detect and remove many streaks from images. Wójcik grants, though, that some observations, such as wide surveys of the sky made just after sunset or before sunrise, are still significantly affected.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would Wójcik (Text 2) most likely respond to Bellini's concern in Text 1?
options: He would argue that satellites in low orbit do not appear in telescope images.

questions.passage: The following text is from Edith Nesbit’s 1902 novel Five Children and It. Five young siblings have just moved with their parents from London to a house in the countryside that they call the White House. It was not really a pretty house at all; it was quite ordinary, and mother thought it was rather inconvenient, and was quite annoyed at there being no shelves, to speak of, and hardly a cupboard in the place. Father used to say that the ironwork on the roof and coping was like an architect’s nightmare. But the house was deep in the country, with no other house in sight, and the children had been in London for two years, without so much as once going to the seaside even for a day by an excursion train, and so the White House seemed to them a sort of Fairy Palace set down in an Earthly Paradise.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although their parents believe the house has several drawbacks, the children are enchanted by it.
The children don’t like the house nearly as much as their parents do.
Each member of the family admires a different characteristic of the house.
The house is beautiful and well built, but the children miss their old home in London.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. In 1910, Rosa works as a telegraph operator in a small town in northern Chile.

Every afternoon the machine on Rosa's desk came alive, tapping out messages from cities she had never seen. Merchants waiting at the counter watched her pencil fly across the paper. When she was hired, the station manager had doubted that a young woman could keep up with the fast operators in Santiago. Now, whenever a long message arrived, he called for Rosa before anyone else. She never mentioned his early doubts, but she let herself smile as she reached for a fresh sheet of paper.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals that Rosa hopes to move to Santiago.
It explains how messages were sent by telegraph.
It shows that the manager has come to trust Rosa's skill.
It suggests that the manager still doubts Rosa's abilities.

questions.passage: “The Poet Walt Whitman” is an 1887 essay by José Martí, a Cuban author and political activist, originally written in Spanish. In the essay, Martí explores the value of literature, arguing that a society’s spiritual well-being depends on the character of its literary culture: ______
questions.question: Which quotation from a translation of “The Poet Walt Whitman” most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Poetry, which brings together or separates, which fortifies or brings anguish, which shores up or demolishes souls, which gives or robs men of faith and vigor, is more necessary to a people than industry itself, for industry provides them with a means of subsistence, while literature gives them the desire and strength for life.”
“Every society brings to literature its own form of expression, and the history of the nations can be told with greater truth by the stages of literature than by chronicles and decades.”

“Where will a race of men go when they have lost the habit of thinking with faith about the scope and meaning of their actions? The best among them, those who consecrate Nature with their sacred desire for the future, will lose, in a sordid and painful annihilation, all stimulus to alleviate the ugliness of humanity.”
“Listen to the song of this hardworking and satisfied nation; listen to Walt Whitman. The exercise of himself exalts him to majesty, tolerance exalts him to justice, and order to joy.”
